_why: The fixed answers the Test Mode student bots write, on the synthetic Business Studies paper (tests/fixtures/bus-practice-paper.json). Deterministic on purpose: the same words go in every run, so a change in what comes back is a change in Marginal, not in the student. Every answer is original text written for this corpus. `expect` is what the offline suite asserts: exact marks where the paper's own key decides (multiple choice, calculation, locally matched marking points), and invariants elsewhere. `stub` is the marker's reply the offline suite feeds the REAL worker code in place of the model, so grounding, reconciliation and refusal run for real; a stub is a stand-in, never a claim about marking quality, and live mode ignores it. `live` is what live mode asserts against the real marker: ranges and orderings, never one exact judgement-based number. `invent` puts a sentence the student did not write into the stubbed review, to prove it never reaches the student as their own words. Version 2 (decision 27): the phrase-matching fixture is a genuinely closed question that declares marking.mode phrase_match, because phrasings alone no longer score anything and phrase matching is refused on an open directive. Every other answer is unchanged from version 1, which stays as it was.

localPoints._why: The synthetic paper's written questions are all open and all go to the marker. This derived paper replaces Question 11(a) with a genuinely CLOSED short answer that declares phrase matching (decision 27), so its marks are decided here, exactly, and the bots keep testing the matcher: an empty answer never scores, a point's description is never a search string, and the matcher's known limits are recorded rather than hidden. It stays at 2 marks so the paper's totals hold.

answers.text:
Kerbside Coffee should roster a second operator on each van from 7am to 9am, the morning peak when the case study says customers complain about waiting.

With two operators, one can take orders while the other makes coffee, so each order is filled sooner at exactly the times the queue forms. Shorter waits should also stop customers walking away, which protects sales during the most valuable two hours of the day.

The strategy adds wage costs, about eight extra casual hours a day across four vans. That cost is limited to the peak, and it is likely to be less than the sales currently lost to the queue, so the second operator is justified.

Executive summary
Online orders at Tidewater Outfitters have grown for three years while store sales have fallen. This report recommends redesigning the warehouse for single online orders, turning two stores into click-and-collect points, and renegotiating the store leases on shorter terms as they expire.

Findings
The warehouse was built to replenish six stores, so it is slow at picking individual online orders, and delivery times have slipped. All six store leases expire within two years, and the owners want to keep every store.

Recommendations
Tidewater should redesign its warehouse layout for single-order picking, which would shorten delivery times for the customers now buying online.
It should keep its six stores but convert two of them into click-and-collect points, so the stores become part of the online sale.
It should renegotiate each lease on a shorter term as it expires.

Conclusion
By changing how the warehouse works and giving the stores a role in online sales, Tidewater can respond to where its customers are buying without closing a store.

answers.text:
Tidewater Outfitters has seen online orders grow for three years while its store sales have fallen, and this shift creates real problems for the business. Its warehouse was built to replenish six stores, so it is slow at picking individual online orders, and delivery times have slipped. At the same time all six store leases expire within two years, although the owners want to keep every store.

The business should redesign its warehouse layout for single-order picking, which would shorten delivery times for the customers now buying online. It should also keep its six stores but convert two of them into click-and-collect points, so the stores become part of the online sale, and it should renegotiate each lease on a shorter term as it expires.

In conclusion, by changing how the warehouse works and giving the stores a role in online sales, Tidewater can respond to where its customers are buying without closing a store.

answers.text:
Marketing is very important for every business. A business I studied used advertising and social media to sell its products and it worked well.

Marketing strategies help businesses to make more money, so they are effective.

stub.summary: States that marketing worked without naming an objective, a real business, or evidence.

across.head: No objective to judge against
across.why: Effectiveness can only be judged against what the marketing was meant to achieve.

answers.text:
Northline Sportswear set a marketing objective of increasing its share of the teenage market, and most of its strategies were chosen to serve that objective. The business moved from print advertising to short video content on social platforms, which reached the age group it was targeting at a lower cost per view than its previous campaigns.

Its second strategy was a loyalty app that gave members early access to new releases. This was effective because it turned occasional buyers into repeat customers, and repeat customers are cheaper to keep than new ones are to find.

However, the business also cut its prices across the range at the same time, which worked against the premium position its advertising was building. A customer who sees the brand as aspirational and then finds it discounted every month will stop believing the first message.

Overall the marketing strategies were effective in achieving the objective they were set, because the business gained share in the group it targeted, but the pricing decision limited how much of that gain it could hold.

stub.summary: Judges strategies against a stated objective and reaches a judgement, but supports effectiveness with assertion rather than evidence.

notices.quote: which reached the age group it was targeting at a lower cost per view than its previous campaigns
notices.head: The comparison is stated but not quantified
notices.why: A figure would turn the claim into evidence.

answers.text:
Northline Sportswear's marketing objective for 2023 was to lift its share of the 13 to 17 year old market from 8 to 12 per cent, and its strategies are best judged against that number.

The move from print to short-form video was effective against that objective. The business reported a cost per view of 4 cents against 19 cents for its print campaigns, and site visits from the target age group rose by a third within six months, so the strategy reached the intended buyers more cheaply.

The loyalty app was also effective, because members bought 2.4 times a year against 1.3 for non-members, which turned reach into repeat purchase. That matters for a share objective, since share held through repeat buying is cheaper to keep than share bought with advertising.

The weakness was price. Northline cut prices across its range in the same year, and its average sale value fell 11 per cent, which undermined the premium image the video campaign was building.

Overall the strategies were largely effective: share reached 11 per cent, close to the target, but the pricing decision cost margin and probably limited how much of the gain will last.

answers.text:
Effective marketing starts with clear objectives, such as increasing market share, building brand awareness or entering a new market. Strategies are then chosen across the marketing mix of product, price, promotion and place.

Promotion through social media is usually effective for younger markets because it is cheap and targeted. Loyalty programs are effective because they increase repeat purchase. Price cuts can increase sales in the short term but can damage a premium brand.

Therefore marketing strategies are effective when they are aligned with the objectives they are meant to achieve.
